title: Question everything
hookLine: Dominican schools teach through structured argument

lines: IT SEEMS THAT GOD DOES NOT EXIST.
cards: It seems that God does not exist. That is how Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar and a saint, opens his own question on whether God exists, in the book he wrote to teach beginners about God.
Before he gives a single argument for God, he lays out objections against. If God is all good, why is there evil? And if nature can explain things on its own, why do we need God at all?
He states them fairly, in plain words, as if a sharp student had raised a hand. Only then does he answer. That way of thinking has a name, and Dominican schools taught by it.

teach.h: A MASTER, A QUESTION, THE OBJECTIONS.
teach.b: You met Thomas, the quiet friar called the dumb ox, back on day eight hundred thirteen; today, his method. A disputation is a structured argument.
In the universities where the friars taught, a master would set a question, students and other masters would raise objections, and then the master would weigh them and give an answer.
The Summa of Thomas Aquinas is built like a disputation on paper. First, the question: whether such and such is so.

teach.h: IT SEEMS THAT. ON THE CONTRARY.
teach.b: Second, the objections, each beginning, it seems that. Third, on the contrary: a voice from scripture or tradition on the other side.

teach.h: I ANSWER THAT. THEN THE REPLIES.
teach.b: Fourth, I answer that: Thomas's own reasoning. And last, the replies, where he goes back to every objection, one by one, often granting what's true in it. So you may not skip the hard question.
You have to say the other side well enough that its friends would recognize it, and answer every objection, not just the weak ones. For Dominicans, this is not doubt for its own sake.
It rests on a conviction that truth can stand being questioned, that faith and reason aren't enemies.

teach.h: PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.
teach.b: Paul puts the instinct in one short line, in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Test first, then hold on.

how: Catholic seminaries and some university philosophy and theology courses still teach the Summa article by article, objections first, and some Dominican houses of study still argue questions out in structured debate.

games.q: you're writing a book to teach beginners about God. you reach the question: does God exist? how do you start?
o: with a list of reasons to believe.
skip the question, since your readers already believe.
games.why: Thomas starts with objections: it seems that God does not exist. only after stating them fairly does he answer.

practice: Bring to mind something you believe firmly, about faith, people, anything, and gently phrase the question a sharp friend might ask against it, beginning the way Thomas does: it seems that.
Don't answer yet; just notice what's true in it, even a little. If you pray, bring the question to God as it is, unfinished.

wordCard.voice: Disputation. A structured argument: the question, the objections stated fairly, the answer, and a reply to every objection. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a disputation, the structured debate of the medieval schools.

carryVoice: Your line: a good question. A good question is the beginning of the answer. Go gently.
